opaque_rectangle_fills.method: Firmware memset preserves r4-r11. Exact installed fill_clipped_gray disassembly has row width in r4, stride in r5, row offset in r6, rows remaining in r7, gray in r9, x1 in r10, x0 at SP+40 and y1 at SP+128. Recovered dimensions cross-checked on all samples. Samples do not count rectangles or prove coverage of earlier clears.

allocation_owners.method: First recovered non-allocator Rust frame, retaining concrete typed destructors. This resolves RawVec growth to its caller; it does not count allocations.

source_findings.finding: shape_run_cached allocates text and owned attributes before lookup; a hit drops the temporary key. Borrowed lookup could avoid hit-path construction/destruction. Hit count and potential savings were not measured.

All 31 recovered allocator samples with shape_fallback as the vector owner share callsite 0x55b018b4 in this capture. Exact binary disassembly confirms reserve for 96-byte elements, consistent with glyphs.reserve(glyph_infos.len()). The function is the regular shaping output path, not proof of font fallback searching.
Batch-end release_shaping_scratch destroys the existing shape-run lookup copies. Removing this work has a memory-retention or repeated-shaping tradeoff; it is not all free savings.

Renderer clears repaint regions white then draws scene quads. All recovered fill_clipped_gray memset samples are white across the screen or reader area. A leading-white-background fast path could skip writes while the cleared region is still pristine; samples alone do not establish scene order or exact savings.

Narrow grayscale rectangles are packed into a reused Vec; full-width grayscale already borrows input. Passing stride/offset to the native direct path could remove the narrow packing copy, measured here at 2.5/3.0 ms forward/backward.

conditions: Eight warm chapter transitions, four each direction; installed release PID 14504; landscape 1680x1264, user-selected 600px column setting. Caller/stack sampling adds overhead, so this capture is for attribution and is not a controlled speed comparison with the earlier portrait capture.
